name: Magnetic Slime That Moves on Its Own
materials: white school glue, liquid starch, iron oxide powder (black), strong neodymium magnet, disposable gloves, mixing bowl, craft stick
steps: Put on disposable gloves. Pour 60 ml of white school glue into the mixing bowl and stir in 2 tablespoons of iron oxide powder until the mixture is uniformly black.
Slowly add liquid starch one tablespoon at a time, stirring continuously until the mixture pulls away from the bowl and forms a stretchy slime. Knead it for 2–3 minutes.
Place the slime on a flat surface and hold the neodymium magnet about 2 cm away without touching it. Watch what happens as you slowly move the magnet closer and then pull it away.
Try dragging the magnet along the table just ahead of the slime and observe how it follows. Experiment with moving the magnet faster or slower to see how the slime responds.
why: Iron oxide powder contains tiny magnetic particles that align and are attracted to the magnetic field produced by the neodymium magnet. The slime's polymer chains (formed when glue cross-links with the borate ions in liquid starch) are flexible enough to let those iron particles drag the whole mass toward the magnet. This combination of polymer chemistry and magnetism is similar to how magnetorheological fluids are used in real-world engineering applications like smart shock absorbers.
safety: Iron oxide powder can stain skin and clothing — wear gloves and old clothes. Keep the neodymium magnet away from electronic devices and credit cards. Adult supervision recommended when handling strong magnets.
next: Try placing a thin sheet of paper or cardboard between the magnet and the slime and test how many sheets it takes before the magnetic attraction can no longer move the slime — this demonstrates how magnetic fields weaken with distance and barriers.

name: Magnetic Cereal: Iron in Your Breakfast
materials: 1 cup iron-fortified breakfast cereal (e.g., Total or Corn Flakes), zip-lock bag, rolling pin, strong neodymium magnet, white paper, water, shallow white bowl
steps: Place one cup of iron-fortified cereal into the zip-lock bag, seal it, and crush the cereal into a fine powder using the rolling pin.
Pour the crushed cereal powder onto a sheet of white paper, then slowly drag the strong magnet back and forth just beneath the paper for about 30 seconds.
Lift the paper and observe any dark specks clinging to the underside near the magnet — these are tiny iron particles pulled from the cereal.

For a clearer result, mix the powder with water in the shallow bowl, stir well, and hold the magnet against the outside of the bowl — watch iron particles migrate toward the magnet through the liquid.
why: Many breakfast cereals are fortified with elemental iron — actual tiny metallic iron particles — as a dietary supplement. Because iron is a ferromagnetic metal, these particles respond to a magnetic field and can be physically separated from the rest of the cereal. This demonstrates that the iron listed on a nutrition label is literally the same element attracted to magnets, just ground into microscopic pieces your body can absorb.
safety: Neodymium magnets are very strong; keep away from electronic devices, credit cards, and young children. Adult supervision recommended when handling strong magnets.
next: Compare different cereal brands by measuring the amount of iron collected from each on a digital kitchen scale. Do cereals with higher iron percentages on the label produce more magnetic material?

name: Soap Film Color Orchestra
materials: wire coat hanger, thin wire or pipe cleaners, dish soap, water, glycerin, shallow tray, black paper or dark backdrop, flashlight or lamp
steps: Mix 1 cup of water with 2 tablespoons of dish soap and 1 tablespoon of glycerin in the shallow tray. Stir gently to avoid bubbles and let it sit for 5 minutes.
Bend thin wire or pipe cleaners into different closed shapes — a circle, square, triangle, and star — leaving a small handle on each.
Dip each wire shape into the soap solution and slowly lift it out to capture a soap film. Hold it in front of the dark backdrop.
Shine the flashlight at the soap film from a slight angle and observe the swirling rainbow colors. Tilt the shape and watch how the colors shift and change over time.
why: Soap films are extremely thin — sometimes just a few hundred nanometers thick. When light hits the film, it reflects off both the front and back surfaces, and these two reflected waves interfere with each other. Depending on the film's thickness at each spot, certain wavelengths (colors) of light are amplified while others cancel out, creating the vivid, shifting rainbow patterns called thin-film interference.
safety: Glycerin and soapy water can make surfaces slippery. Wipe up any spills immediately and keep away from eyes.
next: Try adding a tiny drop of food coloring to the soap mixture and see if it changes which colors appear in the film. Then test whether warmer or cooler water makes the soap film last longer before it pops.

name: Pepper Scatter: Surface Tension Snap
materials: shallow bowl, water, ground black pepper, dish soap, cotton swab
steps: Fill the shallow bowl with about an inch of water and let it settle until the surface is still.
Sprinkle a generous pinch of ground black pepper evenly across the entire water surface so it floats in a thin layer.
Dip just the very tip of the cotton swab into a small drop of dish soap.
Touch the soapy tip gently to the exact center of the water surface and watch what happens to the pepper.
why: Water molecules on the surface pull equally on each other in all directions, creating surface tension that holds the pepper in place. Dish soap breaks those molecular bonds at the point of contact, causing a sudden snap of tension that pulls the water — and the pepper floating on it — racing outward toward the edges of the bowl. The pepper reveals the invisible force of surface tension by showing exactly where it collapses.
safety: Keep soap away from eyes. Adult supervision recommended for very young children.
next: Try touching the center with other substances — a sugar cube, a drop of cooking oil, or a finger dipped in milk — and compare how far and how fast the pepper moves each time.

name: Magnetic Cereal Float
materials: iron-fortified breakfast cereal (like Total or Cheerios), strong neodymium magnet, white bowl, water, ruler
steps: Pour about 2 cups of water into the white bowl and place a single piece of iron-fortified cereal on the surface so it floats.
Hold the neodymium magnet just above the water surface near the cereal piece — do not touch the water — and slowly move it in a circle.
Observe whether the cereal follows the magnet. Try moving it faster and slower and record what you notice.
Crush several pieces of cereal into fine powder, sprinkle it on the water, and repeat the magnet test to see if the effect is stronger or weaker.
why: Iron-fortified cereals contain tiny particles of elemental iron metal mixed into the grain during manufacturing. Iron is ferromagnetic, meaning its atoms align with an external magnetic field and are physically attracted to it. When the cereal floats on water with minimal friction, even a weak magnetic force is enough to drag the iron-containing cereal toward the magnet.
safety: Neodymium magnets are very strong and can pinch skin or shatter if two snap together — keep them away from younger children and electronics.
next: Try the same experiment with cereals that list iron lower on the nutrition label and compare how far away the magnet must be to still move them — create a bar chart of magnet distance vs. iron content (mg per serving).
